newsitem.title: CANADA: INSTANT VIEW-Canada CPI rises 2.2 percent on year.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW-Canada CPI rises 2.2 percent on year.

text.p: Following are reactions to consumer price data released by Statistics Canada on Friday. Canada's unadjusted February consumer price index rose 0.1 percent in the month and 2.2 percent in the year to 137.3, Statistics Canada said Friday. Core CPI rose 1.5 percent year-on-year.

Economists in a Reuters survey had forecast, on average, the seasonally adjusted CPI to rise 0.1 percent on the month and the undadjusted CPI to rise 0.2 percent on the month. The survey also forecast a 2.2 percent year-over-year rise in the all-items and a 1.7 percent increase in the core CPI.
Michael Gregory, economist, Lehman Brothers - "A little bit of surprise in terms of the core drifting down a little bit here from 1.8 (percent) to 1.5 (percent) on a year-over-year basis.
"It shows that inflation is not a problem right now in the Canadian economy and there is enough slack to more than absorb the growth we've been seeing lately.
"I think marginally this number lowers the probability of the Bank (of Canada) following (a Federal Reserve rate rise) because inflation is still very good on the ground as it stands right now.
Mullins - "The bottom line here is the inflation processes that central banks worry about are sometime in the future.
"The Bank (of Canada) may sit on their hands (in the event of a Federal Reserve rate rise). It's purely a function of the currency strength.
"But if I were to bet, I would say the Bank of Canada will not follow (the Fed) next week."
Paul Ferley, assistant chief economist, Bank of Montreal -- "The overall rate came within our expected range at 2.2 percent (year-over-year).
Ferley - "But the core dropping to 1.5 (percent) was sort of lower than what we had expected.
"Our feeling is that it reflects the continuing slack in the Canadian economy continuing to exert downward pressure on inflation.

"Certainly it implies the domestic reasons are not there to raise interest rates. As long as the Canadian dollar holds in there, I think the Bank (of Canada) would try to resist any pressure coming from the United States."
